short: Government policies that shield domestic producers from foreign competition, using tariffs, quotas, subsidies or rules that make imports harder or costlier.
kid: Imagine your town says lemonade from the next town must pay a big extra charge to be sold here. That helps the town's own lemonade stands, but everyone may pay more for a cup.
detail: Protectionism is any policy that favours domestic producers by restricting imports or raising their cost. Tools include tariffs, import quotas, licensing, subsidies for local firms, local-content rules and product standards written to keep foreign goods out. Supporters argue it protects jobs, young industries and national security; critics point out that consumers and downstream firms pay higher prices, inefficient producers survive and trading partners usually retaliate. For markets, rising protectionism hurts exporters and firms with global supply chains, and can push up inflation. The US tariff increases of 2018 and 2025 are recent examples; India has used higher customs duties and import substitution at various times, alongside schemes such as Production Linked Incentives. A common confusion: protectionism is not a reliable cure for a trade deficit. Tariffs often shift where imports come from rather than shrinking the overall deficit, which depends on national saving and investment.
example: Say an imported solar panel costs $100 and a 25% tariff is added, so it sells for $125. A local maker charging $118 can now win the order, but the buyer pays $18 more than the old import price.

short: Any rule other than a tariff that restricts imports, such as quotas, licences, product standards, testing requirements or slow customs procedures.
kid: Instead of making visitors pay at the gate, the club says their toys must be a certain colour and checked for a week first. Fewer visitors bother to come in.
detail: A non-tariff barrier (NTB) restricts trade through means other than a customs duty. Examples include import quotas, licensing, food-safety and technical standards, mandatory certification, local-content rules, rules of origin and slow or costly border procedures. The WTO prefers the neutral term non-tariff measures (NTMs), because many such rules serve genuine public purposes; they become barriers when they are stricter than needed or applied unevenly. As average tariffs have fallen, NTBs are often the bigger hurdle for exporters. Indian exporters regularly cite strict pesticide-residue limits on farm goods in some markets, while trading partners have flagged India's Quality Control Orders, which require certification by the Bureau of Indian Standards for many imports. Confusion to avoid: an FTA that cuts tariffs to zero does not fully open a market, because NTBs can still block access, which is why trade talks also negotiate standards and mutual recognition.
example: Say a country cuts its tariff on imported toys to zero but requires every shipment to be lab-tested at $2,000 per batch. For an exporter sending batches worth $20,000, the test alone adds 10% to cost, as much as a 10% tariff.

short: An extra import tax charged on goods a foreign firm sells below its home-market price or below cost, to offset that unfair low pricing.
kid: A big shop from far away sells cookies here for less than they cost to make, so local bakers cannot keep up. The town adds a charge on those cookies to make things fair again.
detail: Dumping happens when an exporter sells in a foreign market below its normal value, usually its domestic selling price or its cost of production. Under WTO rules, an importing country may impose an anti-dumping duty if an investigation shows dumping and material injury to its domestic industry. The duty is generally capped at the dumping margin, the gap between normal value and export price, and typically lasts five years, subject to review. In India, the Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) investigates and recommends duties, and the Finance Ministry decides whether to impose them; India is among the heaviest users of anti-dumping action, often on chemicals and steel from China. For investors, a new duty can lift domestic producers' prices and margins while raising input costs for user industries. Confusion to avoid: a countervailing duty is different, because it targets foreign government subsidies rather than a firm's low pricing.
example: Say a chemical sells for ₹100 per kg in its home country but is exported to India at ₹80 per kg. The dumping margin is ₹20, or 25% of the export price, so India can impose a duty of up to ₹20 per kg.
formula: Dumping margin = (Normal value - Export price) / Export price

short: An extra import duty that offsets subsidies a foreign government gave its exporters, so subsidised goods cannot unfairly undercut local producers.
kid: If another town's grown-ups secretly pay for their children's paint, those children can sell drawings very cheaply. Our town adds a small charge to their drawings so things stay fair.
detail: A countervailing duty (CVD), also called an anti-subsidy duty, is levied on imports that benefit from subsidies in the exporting country, such as cheap state loans, tax breaks, export grants or below-market inputs. The WTO Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures allows it when an investigation finds a specific subsidy that causes material injury to the importing country's industry, and the duty may not exceed the subsidy per unit. In India, the DGTR runs these investigations alongside anti-dumping cases. The key difference: anti-dumping duties target a firm's pricing, while countervailing duties target government support, and both can apply to the same product. Separately, older Indian customs law used CVD for an additional duty matching domestic excise, which GST largely replaced; do not mix the two meanings. For investors, these duties lift prices for protected domestic producers and raise costs for the industries that buy the product.
example: Say a foreign government gives steel exporters a subsidy worth $40 per tonne on steel exported at $500 per tonne. The importing country can levy a countervailing duty of up to $40 per tonne, which is 8% of the export price.
formula: Maximum countervailing duty per unit = Subsidy per unit

short: A temporary import duty or quota used when a sudden surge of imports seriously harms domestic producers, even if the trade itself is fair.
kid: If a huge pile of balloons suddenly arrives from everywhere and local balloon sellers cannot sell any, the town adds a small charge on new balloons for a while so local sellers can catch their breath.
detail: A safeguard duty is a temporary trade remedy allowed by the WTO Agreement on Safeguards when imports rise so sharply, in absolute terms or relative to domestic output, that they cause or threaten serious injury to a domestic industry. Unlike anti-dumping or countervailing duties, no unfair practice has to be shown, so the injury test is stricter, and the measure applies to imports from all sources rather than one country, apart from exemptions for small developing-country suppliers. Safeguards are meant to give the industry time to adjust: WTO rules limit them to four years, extendable to eight in total, and expect them to be phased down. India's DGTR investigates safeguard cases too, with steel a frequent subject, and the US used safeguard tariffs on washing machines and solar panels in 2018. Confusion to avoid: a safeguard does not punish anyone's behaviour; it responds to a surge.
example: Say imports of a steel product jump from 10 lakh tonnes to 25 lakh tonnes in a year and local mills cut output. A 12% safeguard duty raises the landed cost of a ₹50,000 per tonne import to ₹56,000, giving mills room to recover.

short: A treaty where two or more countries cut or remove tariffs and other barriers on most goods, and often services, traded between them.
kid: Two friends promise to swap snacks without asking for anything extra each time. Because swapping is easy, they share more snacks than before.
detail: A free trade agreement (FTA) is a treaty in which members eliminate or sharply reduce tariffs on substantially all trade between them, usually over a phase-in period, while each keeps its own tariffs towards outsiders. Modern FTAs also cover services, investment, government procurement, intellectual property and standards. Because members keep separate external tariffs, FTAs need rules of origin to stop goods being routed through the lowest-tariff member. India's agreements include those with ASEAN, Japan, South Korea, the UAE (in force 2022), Australia, the European Free Trade Association and the UK (signed 2025); the names vary, but the idea is the same. FTAs are a permitted exception to the WTO's most-favoured-nation rule. For investors, an FTA can help exporters such as textiles or gems and jewellery while exposing protected industries to competition. Confusion to avoid: an FTA is not a customs union, where members also share a common external tariff.
example: Say India imports a machine worth $10,000 that normally attracts a 7.5% duty, or $750. Under an FTA with zero duty on that product, the importer saves the full $750, provided the machine meets the rules of origin.

short: The criteria that decide which country a product legally comes from, which sets the tariff it pays and whether trade-deal benefits apply.
kid: A cake counts as your class's cake only if your class did most of the mixing and baking, not just added the cherry on top. Only then does your class win the prize.
detail: Rules of origin decide a good's economic nationality. Non-preferential rules are used for things like anti-dumping duties, quotas and origin labelling; preferential rules decide whether a product qualifies for lower tariffs under a free trade agreement. Common tests are wholly obtained (for example, crops grown in the country), a change in tariff classification after processing, and a minimum regional value content, such as 35% or 40% of value added locally. Without them, goods from a non-member could be routed through a partner with a lower tariff to dodge duty, a practice called transshipment or circumvention. For companies, meeting origin rules means tracing suppliers and keeping certificates of origin, a compliance cost that leads many firms not to use FTA benefits at all. US tariff policy in 2025 also targeted transshipment. Confusion to avoid: a 'Made in' label on packaging is not by itself proof of origin for customs.
example: Say a phone assembled in Country A sells for $200 and uses $150 of parts imported from Country C, so only $50, or 25%, is value added in A. If the FTA requires 35% regional value content, the phone does not qualify for the zero tariff and pays the normal duty.
formula: Regional value content = (Transaction value - Value of non-originating materials) / Transaction value x 100

short: A rule that a country must offer every World Trade Organization member the same best tariff and treatment it gives any other member.
kid: If you give one friend two sweets, you must give every friend in the club two sweets too. No secret favourites.
detail: Most favoured nation (MFN) treatment, set out in Article I of the GATT, requires each WTO member to extend any tariff cut or trade advantage given to one member immediately and unconditionally to all members. Despite the name, it means equal treatment, not special treatment, and a country's MFN tariff is simply its standard duty for WTO members. The main exceptions are free trade agreements and customs unions, preferences for developing countries, and trade remedies such as anti-dumping duties. Withdrawing MFN status is a strong signal: India withdrew it from Pakistan in 2019 after the Pulwama attack, and the US and several allies revoked Russia's in 2022. The term also appears outside trade, for example in contracts and in US drug-pricing policy, where it means matching the lowest price offered elsewhere. Confusion to avoid: MFN rates are often higher than the rates a country charges its FTA partners.
example: Say India's MFN duty on a product is 10% and an FTA partner pays 0%. An importer bringing in ₹10 lakh of the product from a non-FTA WTO member pays ₹1 lakh in duty, while the same shipment from the FTA partner pays nothing.

short: The Geneva-based international body that sets global trade rules, hosts trade negotiations and settles trade disputes among its more than 160 members.
kid: It is like the referee for a big playground game between countries. It writes the rules for swapping things and helps when two players argue.
detail: The World Trade Organization (WTO), set up in 1995 to succeed the GATT, runs the multilateral trading system. Its core principles are non-discrimination (most-favoured-nation and national treatment), bound tariff ceilings and transparency. Members negotiate at ministerial conferences that decide by consensus, which makes new deals slow. Its dispute settlement system lets members challenge each other's measures, but the Appellate Body, its appeals court, has been unable to hear cases since December 2019 because the US has blocked new appointments, so a losing party can appeal into a void. India, a founding member, has used the WTO to defend food-security stockholding and farm support, and has lost cases over its export subsidies and its tariffs on some electronics. For markets, WTO rulings can authorise retaliatory tariffs. Confusion to avoid: the WTO does not set countries' tariffs; members bind their own ceilings and agree to stay under them.
example: Say a country has bound its tariff on a product at 40% at the WTO but currently applies 20%. It can legally raise the applied rate to 40%, doubling the duty on a $1,000 shipment from $200 to $400, but going to 50% would breach its commitment.

short: The ability to make a good while giving up less of other goods than another producer would; it is why trade can benefit both sides.
kid: Mum bakes and folds clothes faster than you, but she is much, much faster at baking. If she bakes and you fold, the whole job gets done sooner.
detail: Comparative advantage, set out by David Ricardo in 1817, says a country gains by specialising in goods it can produce at the lowest opportunity cost, meaning what it gives up to make them, and trading for the rest. It differs from absolute advantage, which is producing more with the same resources. Even a country that is more productive at everything gains from trade, because its workers and capital are best used where its edge is largest. This is the core argument for free trade. India's comparative advantage in IT and business services, built on a skilled, English-speaking workforce, is a classic example, as is Bangladesh's in garments. Comparative advantage can shift over time with skills, technology and policy. Confusion to avoid: it does not mean being the cheapest or best producer; a country can lack an absolute advantage in every good and still have a comparative advantage in some.
example: Say in one day India can make 10 software units or 5 machines, while Germany can make 6 software units or 6 machines. One software unit costs India 0.5 machine but costs Germany 1 machine, so India should specialise in software and Germany in machines, and trading lets both have more of each.
formula: Opportunity cost of good X = Units of good Y given up / Units of good X gained

short: A global organisation of about 190 member countries that monitors economies, lends to countries running short of foreign currency and advises on policy.
kid: It is like a shared piggy bank for many families. If one family runs out of money for important things, it can borrow from the piggy bank, but it must promise to spend more carefully.
detail: The International Monetary Fund (IMF), created at Bretton Woods in 1944 and based in Washington, promotes international monetary stability. It does three main things: surveillance, reviewing each member's economy in regular Article IV reports and publishing the World Economic Outlook; lending, usually to countries facing a balance of payments crisis, with conditions such as fiscal tightening or reforms; and technical help. Members contribute through quotas, which also set their voting power and access to loans, and the IMF issues Special Drawing Rights. India borrowed from the IMF in its 1991 crisis, a programme linked to the liberalisation that followed; Sri Lanka and Pakistan have had programmes more recently. For markets, an IMF deal often calms investors because it brings money and policy discipline. Confusion to avoid: the IMF is not the World Bank. The IMF deals with macroeconomic and currency stability, while the World Bank funds long-term development.
example: Say a country's foreign exchange reserves have fallen to $8 billion, under two months of imports at $5 billion a month. An IMF programme of $3 billion, paid in instalments as reform targets are met, would lift reserves to $11 billion once fully paid, about 2.2 months of imports, buying time.

short: An international reserve asset created by the IMF, valued from a basket of five major currencies, that member countries can swap for usable currencies.
kid: Think of special tokens a club gives its members. You cannot spend them in a shop, but you can swap them with another member for real coins when you need them.
detail: Special drawing rights (SDRs), created by the IMF in 1969, are an international reserve asset allocated to member countries in proportion to their IMF quotas. An SDR is not a currency and not a claim on the IMF; it is a potential claim on members' freely usable currencies, which countries can obtain through voluntary trading arrangements. Its value is set daily from a basket of the US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen and pound sterling, reviewed every five years. The SDR is also the IMF's unit of account, and the SDR interest rate is charged on IMF loans. The largest allocation, about SDR 456 billion (roughly $650 billion), came in August 2021 to help countries through the pandemic; India received about SDR 12.6 billion. SDR holdings form part of India's foreign exchange reserves. Confusion to avoid: XDR is simply the currency code for the SDR, not a separate asset.
example: Say the SDR is worth $1.35 and a country holds SDR 10 billion. Its holdings count as $13.5 billion of reserves, and it can swap them with another IMF member for dollars or euros if needed.
formula: SDR value in dollars = Sum of (amount of each currency in the basket x dollar value of that currency)

aliases: Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication
hl: society for worldwide interbank financial telecommunication
short: A Belgium-based cooperative running the secure messaging network banks use to send each other payment instructions; it does not move money itself.
kid: It is like a very safe post office that carries notes between big money houses. The note says who should get paid, and then the houses move the money themselves.
detail: SWIFT, the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, is a member-owned cooperative founded in 1973 and based in Belgium. It connects more than 11,000 financial institutions in over 200 countries and territories with standardised, secure messages for payments, securities and trade finance. Each institution has a SWIFT code, also called a BIC, that identifies it in cross-border transfers. SWIFT carries instructions only; the money itself moves through correspondent bank accounts and settlement systems. Because it is so central, disconnecting a country's banks from SWIFT is a powerful sanction: Iranian banks were cut off in 2012, and several major Russian banks in 2022. This has encouraged alternatives such as Russia's SPFS and China's CIPS. Confusion to avoid: SWIFT is not a bank or a payment system, and being cut off does not by itself freeze anyone's money.
example: Say an Indian exporter is owed $50,000 by a US buyer. The buyer's bank sends a SWIFT message to the exporter's bank in Mumbai, the dollars settle through correspondent accounts, and at an assumed ₹85 per dollar the exporter receives ₹42.5 lakh before charges.

short: How freely a currency can be swapped for foreign currency, either for trade and travel only or also for moving investments across borders.
kid: Some play money can be swapped for real coins only to buy snacks at the fair. Other play money can be swapped for anything you like, any time.
detail: Convertibility describes how freely residents and non-residents can exchange a currency for foreign currency at market rates. Current account convertibility covers payments for trade in goods and services, interest, dividends and remittances; capital account convertibility also covers buying and selling assets across borders, such as shares, bonds, property and loans. Full convertibility means both are free. India made the rupee convertible on the current account in August 1994, when it accepted the IMF's Article VIII obligations, but its capital account is only partly open: foreign investment, overseas borrowing and residents' outward remittances operate within limits set under FEMA. The Tarapore committees of 1997 and 2006 laid out roadmaps towards fuller capital account convertibility, which India has followed gradually. More openness can attract investment, but it raises exposure to hot money and sudden outflows. Confusion to avoid: convertibility is not about whether the exchange rate is fixed or floating.
example: Say an Indian resident wants to invest $300,000 in foreign shares in one year. Under the rules as of 2025, the Liberalised Remittance Scheme allows $250,000 per financial year, so $50,000 must wait for the next year: the capital account is open, but only partly.

short: Government rules that limit or tax money moving into or out of a country, such as caps on foreign investment, borrowing abroad or remittances.
kid: Grown-ups put a gate on the toy box so toys cannot be carried off to other houses too fast, or brought in all at once.
detail: Capital controls restrict cross-border flows of investment and lending through outright limits, approvals, minimum holding periods or taxes on inflows or outflows. They can target inflows, to stop speculative money inflating asset prices and the currency, or outflows, to stop a panic from draining reserves. The IMF, once sceptical, now accepts them as capital flow management measures in some situations, preferably temporary and alongside sound policy. Examples include Malaysia's outflow controls in 1998, Brazil's tax on foreign portfolio inflows from 2009 and Iceland's controls after its 2008 banking collapse. India manages its capital account through FEMA: sector caps on FDI, limits on foreign holdings of government bonds, rules on external commercial borrowing and the Liberalised Remittance Scheme for residents. Controls can shield an economy but can also deter investors and encourage evasion. Confusion to avoid: capital controls usually leave payments for imports alone; those belong to the current account.
example: Say a country levies a 2% tax on foreign money entering its bond market. A foreign investor bringing in $10 million pays $200,000 upfront, which wipes out a 1% yearly interest-rate advantage for two years and discourages short-term flows.

short: Short-term investment money that moves quickly between countries chasing higher interest rates or quick gains, and can leave just as fast.
kid: Some visitors come to the fair only for the best free sweets. The moment another fair offers better sweets, they all run off together.
detail: Hot money is short-term, highly mobile capital that crosses borders in search of higher interest rates, expected currency gains or quick equity profits. It typically flows through foreign portfolio investment in bonds and shares, short-term bank deposits and carry trades, rather than factories or long-term stakes. Inflows can lift asset prices and strengthen the currency; reversals can drain reserves, weaken the currency and hit markets hard, as in the 2013 taper tantrum, when the rupee slid to record lows after the US Federal Reserve hinted at slowing its bond purchases. Policymakers watch it because it can amplify booms and busts, and may respond by building reserves, tightening prudential rules or using capital controls. India prefers FDI to portfolio flows partly for this reason. Confusion to avoid: not all foreign portfolio money is hot money; long-horizon pension and index funds tend to be much stickier.
example: Say a foreign fund borrows at 1% abroad and buys Indian bonds yielding 7%, earning a 6-point gap: $6 million a year on $100 million. If the rupee falls 8% against the funding currency, the $8 million currency loss exceeds the whole year's gain, so such money tends to leave at the first sign of rupee weakness.

short: A contract to settle in dollars only the gain or loss on a currency's future exchange rate, without ever exchanging that currency itself.
kid: Two friends guess how many marbles a jar will hold next week. They never touch the marbles; whoever guessed wrong just gives the other a few sweets.
detail: A non-deliverable forward (NDF) is a forward contract on a currency that is restricted or not fully convertible, such as the Indian rupee, Chinese yuan or Brazilian real, in which that currency never changes hands. At maturity the two sides compare the agreed rate with an official fixing, such as the FBIL reference rate for the rupee, and settle only the difference, usually in US dollars. NDFs let foreign investors hedge or speculate without using the onshore market. The offshore rupee NDF market, centred in Singapore, Dubai, London and New York, is large, and rupee moves often begin there overnight, which is why traders check NDF levels before Indian markets open. Since 2020 the RBI has gradually let Indian banks deal in rupee NDFs, narrowing gaps between onshore and offshore rates. Confusion to avoid: an NDF is not a deliverable forward; the principal amount is never exchanged.
example: Say a fund buys a one-month dollar-rupee NDF for $10 million at ₹86.00. If the fixing at maturity is ₹87.00, the rupee has weakened and the fund receives the difference of ₹1 crore, converted at the fixing into about $114,943, without any rupees changing hands.
formula: NDF settlement in dollars = Notional in dollars x (Fixing rate - Contract rate) / Fixing rate

short: A deal to exchange two currencies now and swap them back on a future date at a pre-agreed rate, like borrowing one currency against another.
kid: You lend your friend your toy car today, and she lends you her doll. Next week you each give the toys back, plus a small extra treat to make it fair.
detail: An FX swap combines a spot foreign exchange trade with an opposite forward trade: one side buys a currency today and agrees to sell it back on a set date at a forward rate fixed now. The gap between the two rates, called swap points, reflects the interest rate difference between the currencies. FX swaps are the most traded instrument in global currency markets, used by banks to fund one currency with another and by companies to roll over hedges. Central banks use them too: in a buy/sell swap, the RBI buys dollars from banks now, adding rupee liquidity, and sells them back later, as it did in 2019 and early 2025. Confusion to avoid: an FX swap is not a cross-currency swap. An FX swap exchanges principal twice with no periodic interest payments and is usually short-term, while a cross-currency swap also exchanges interest payments, often over years.
example: Say a bank sells $100 million to the RBI at a spot rate of ₹85.00 and agrees to buy it back in one year at ₹87.50. It receives ₹850 crore now and pays ₹875 crore later; the ₹25 crore difference, about 2.9%, is the premium it pays for the rupee funding.
formula: Forward rate = Spot rate x (1 + Domestic interest rate x t) / (1 + Foreign interest rate x t); Swap points = Forward rate - Spot rate

short: The idea that a higher interest rate in one currency is cancelled out by that currency's expected or locked-in fall, leaving no free profit.
kid: One friend gives you more stickers for keeping your toy at her house, but her stickers are smaller. In the end, both offers fill your sticker book by the same amount.
detail: Covered interest parity (CIP) says the forward premium or discount on a currency equals the interest rate difference, so borrowing in one currency, converting, investing in another and locking the return with a forward contract yields no riskless profit. Arbitrage keeps it close to true in liquid markets, though small gaps have persisted since 2008 because of banks' balance-sheet costs. Uncovered interest parity (UIP) says the expected change in the spot rate should offset the rate gap without any hedge; it often fails, which is why carry trades tend to pay on average, until sharp reversals. CIP explains why the dollar usually trades at a forward premium against the rupee: Indian interest rates are higher, so forward dollars cost more rupees. Confusion to avoid: a forward rate is not a forecast; under CIP it is arithmetic from the spot rate and two interest rates.
example: Say spot is ₹85.00 per dollar, one-year rupee interest is 6.5% and dollar interest is 4.5%. Covered parity gives a one-year forward rate of 85 x 1.065 / 1.045 = ₹86.63, a premium of about 1.9%, close to the 2-point rate gap.
formula: Forward rate = Spot rate x (1 + Domestic interest rate) / (1 + Foreign interest rate), with rates for the contract period and the exchange rate quoted as domestic currency per unit of foreign currency

short: The theory that exchange rates should adjust until the same basket of goods costs the same everywhere; also used to compare countries' living standards.
kid: If a toy costs 2 coins here and 10 shells on the island, then 1 coin should swap for 5 shells. Then the toy costs the same wherever you buy it.
detail: Purchasing power parity (PPP) starts from the law of one price: identical goods should cost the same in different countries once converted into a common currency. Absolute PPP says the exchange rate equals the ratio of price levels; relative PPP says a currency with higher inflation should weaken by roughly the inflation gap over time. In practice exchange rates stray from PPP for years because of transport costs, tariffs, non-traded services and capital flows, so PPP is a long-run anchor, not a short-term forecast. World Bank PPP rates are used to compare GDP and incomes. Because many goods and services are cheaper in India, its GDP is several times larger in PPP terms than at market exchange rates, ranking it third in the world on that basis as of 2025. Confusion to avoid: PPP figures do not show what Indian incomes or assets are worth in dollars on the market.
example: Say a basket of goods costs ₹4,000 in India and $100 in the US, giving a PPP rate of ₹40 per dollar. If the market rate is ₹85, a $100 salary converted at market rates gives ₹8,500, enough to buy the basket more than twice over in India.
formula: PPP exchange rate = Price of basket in domestic currency / Price of same basket in foreign currency; relative PPP: expected % change in exchange rate = approximately Domestic inflation - Foreign inflation

short: The Economist's light-hearted gauge of whether currencies are over- or undervalued, comparing the price of a McDonald's Big Mac burger across countries.
kid: If the same burger costs much less in one country than another, that country's coins might be worth more than people think. It is a fun way to compare money using one snack.
detail: Created by The Economist in 1986, the Big Mac Index applies purchasing power parity to a single, widely sold product. Dividing a country's local Big Mac price by the US price gives an implied exchange rate; comparing that with the actual market rate suggests whether the currency is over- or undervalued. Because burgers are made with local labour, rent and ingredients, the index also captures differences in living costs, so poorer countries' currencies almost always look undervalued; The Economist therefore publishes a GDP-adjusted version too. For India it uses the Maharaja Mac, a chicken burger, since beef is not on the menu. The index is a teaching tool, not a trading signal, and currencies can stay far from burger parity for decades. Confusion to avoid: a cheap Big Mac does not mean a currency is about to rise; it often reflects lower wages and rents rather than mispricing.
example: Take hypothetical round prices, not actual menu prices: if the burger costs $6.00 in the US and ₹300 in India, the implied rate is 300 / 6 = ₹50 per dollar. With the market rate at ₹80, the index would say the rupee is 37.5% undervalued, since 50 / 80 - 1 = -0.375.
formula: Implied exchange rate = Local Big Mac price / US Big Mac price; Over(+) or under(-) valuation = Implied rate / Market rate - 1

short: Money Indian companies borrow from foreign lenders or bond investors, usually in foreign currency, within limits and conditions set by the RBI.
kid: Sometimes a shop borrows coins from a friend in another town because that friend asks for less back. But if the other town's coins become dearer, paying back gets harder.
detail: External commercial borrowings (ECBs) are commercial loans, bonds and similar instruments raised by eligible Indian entities from recognised non-resident lenders. The RBI regulates them under FEMA, setting who may borrow and lend, minimum average maturity, a ceiling on all-in cost over a benchmark rate, barred end uses (such as real estate speculation) and how much can be raised under the automatic route versus the approval route. These conditions are revised from time to time, so check the current RBI master direction. ECBs can be in foreign currency or in rupees, the latter including masala bonds. Companies use them when global interest rates plus hedging costs undercut domestic borrowing. The key risk is currency mismatch: a firm earning in rupees with unhedged dollar debt sees its repayments jump if the rupee falls. Confusion to avoid: in global news, ECB usually means the European Central Bank.
example: Say ABC Ltd borrows $10 million at 6% when the rupee is ₹80 per dollar, a ₹80 crore loan. If the rupee weakens to ₹88 by repayment, the principal alone costs ₹88 crore, an ₹8 crore loss that outweighs more than three years of interest saved against a 9% rupee loan (₹2.4 crore a year).

short: An RBI scheme letting Indian residents send money abroad each financial year, up to a set limit, for travel, study, gifts or overseas investment.
kid: Each year, every child may take up to a certain number of marbles out of the house to play or swap with friends in other towns. Grown-ups keep count.
detail: The Liberalised Remittance Scheme, introduced by the RBI in 2004, lets resident individuals, including minors, send money abroad without prior approval for permitted current and capital account purposes: travel, education, medical treatment, gifts, support of relatives, and investment in foreign shares, funds or property. The limit started at $25,000 and, under the rules as of 2025, is $250,000 per person per financial year. Banks collect tax at source on many remittances above a threshold, which can be adjusted against income tax; rates and thresholds change with budgets. LRS cannot be used for margin trading, lotteries or betting, or for sending money to countries flagged as non-cooperative by the Financial Action Task Force. It is the main legal route for Indians to buy foreign stocks or funds directly. Confusion to avoid: the limit applies per individual, not per family, and tax collected at source is an advance, not an extra tax.
example: Under the rules as of 2025, an Indian resident can remit up to $250,000 a year. Say she spends $40,000 on her child's tuition abroad and $60,000 on US index funds; she can still remit $150,000 more before the financial year ends.

short: Using contracts that fix in advance the exchange rate for future foreign-currency payments or receipts, to avoid losses if the rate moves.
kid: You agree today with a friend that next week you will swap 10 stickers for 5 marbles, no matter what. Even if marbles become rare, your swap is safe.
detail: Currency hedging protects the home-currency value of future cash flows, assets or debts from exchange rate moves. Tools include forwards, which lock in a rate; currency futures; options, which cap losses but keep upside; and natural hedges, such as matching dollar costs and revenue. An Indian IT exporter earning dollars hedges against a stronger rupee, while an oil importer or a company with dollar loans hedges against a weaker one. For Indian importers and dollar borrowers, the cost is roughly the forward premium, which reflects the interest rate gap; exporters selling forward earn it but forgo gains if the rupee weakens. Unhedged exposure is the part left open; the RBI asks banks to watch it in borrowers, since a sharp rupee fall can cause defaults. Confusion to avoid: hedging is not about profiting from currency moves; a good hedge can lose money, offset by a gain on the underlying flow.
example: Say an exporter expects $1 million in three months and sells it forward at ₹86. If the rupee strengthens to ₹83, it still receives ₹8.6 crore instead of ₹8.3 crore; if the rupee weakens to ₹89, it gives up the extra ₹30 lakh, which is the price of certainty.

short: How much a change in the exchange rate shows up in the prices of imports and, in turn, in a country's overall inflation.
kid: If your money buys fewer crayons from far away than before, crayons in the shop cost more. Soon other things made with those crayons may cost more too.
detail: Exchange rate pass-through measures how far a currency move carries through to prices. First-stage pass-through is to import prices; second-stage is to producer and consumer prices. If the rupee cost of a dollar rises 10% and import prices rise 10% in rupees, pass-through to import prices is complete; if consumer inflation then rises only 1 percentage point, pass-through to consumer prices is about 0.1. It tends to be higher for commodities priced in dollars, such as crude oil, gold and edible oils, which loom large in India's imports, and lower when importers absorb costs, inflation expectations are well anchored or prices are set in local currency. Studies of India have generally found modest pass-through to consumer prices. Central banks weigh it when judging whether a weak currency threatens their inflation target. Confusion to avoid: pass-through also describes how policy rate changes reach lending rates; this entry is about currencies.
example: Say the rupee falls from ₹80 to ₹88 per dollar, a 10% rise in the rupee cost of a dollar. Crude at $80 a barrel now costs ₹7,040 instead of ₹6,400, a 10% jump, but if retail inflation rises only 0.8 percentage point, pass-through to consumer prices is 0.08.
formula: Pass-through coefficient = % change in domestic prices / % change in exchange rate

short: When a government or central bank deliberately pushes its currency's value, usually weaker, to gain an unfair trade edge, often through heavy market intervention.
kid: Imagine a shop that secretly makes its price tags look smaller so everyone buys from it instead of the others. The other shops say that is not fair.
detail: Currency manipulation means a country deliberately steers its exchange rate, typically holding it down, to make its exports cheaper and imports dearer. IMF rules forbid manipulation aimed at gaining an unfair competitive advantage. In practice the label comes mostly from the US Treasury's semi-annual currency report, which, under the criteria as of 2025, tests major trading partners for a goods and services trade surplus with the US of at least $15 billion, a current account surplus of at least 3% of GDP, and persistent one-sided foreign exchange buying, in at least 8 of 12 months, worth at least 2% of GDP. Meeting two criteria puts a country on the monitoring list; a formal designation needs further judgement. Treasury labelled China a manipulator in August 2019 and dropped the label in January 2020. Confusion to avoid: intervention to smooth volatility, as the RBI describes its own, is not manipulation.
example: Say a country has GDP of $500 billion and its central bank makes net purchases of foreign currency in 9 of 12 months, totalling $15 billion. That is 3% of GDP, above the 2% threshold in the US Treasury criteria as of 2025, so the intervention test would be met.

short: The idea that a country cannot at once fix its exchange rate, let money flow freely across borders and set its own interest rates.
kid: You have three wishes, but the genie only grants two at a time. If you want the third, you must give up one of the others.
detail: The impossible trinity, or monetary trilemma, from the Mundell-Fleming model, says a country can have at most two of three things: a fixed exchange rate, free cross-border capital flows and an independent monetary policy. With free capital flows and a peg, interest rates must follow the anchor country's, as Hong Kong's do with the US. To keep its own rates and a peg, a country needs capital controls, the route China has largely taken. To have open capital flows and its own rates, it must let the currency float, as the US and the euro area do. India runs a middle path: a managed float, a partly open capital account and an inflation-targeting RBI, using large reserves to smooth the rupee. Confusion to avoid: the trilemma describes the pure versions of each goal; in practice countries trade off partial degrees of each, and reserves can buy only temporary room.
example: Say a country pegs its currency to the dollar and allows free capital flows. If US interest rates rise from 4% to 5% while this central bank holds at 4%, money moves into dollars and drains its reserves until it raises rates, imposes capital controls or abandons the peg.

short: Income a country earns by selling services, such as software, consulting, tourism, shipping and finance, to customers abroad.
kid: Instead of selling toys to children in other towns, you help them fix their toys or teach them a game, and they pay you for your help.
detail: Services exports are sales of services by residents to non-residents, recorded in the current account of the balance of payments. They include software and IT-enabled services, business and professional services, spending by foreign tourists, transport, insurance, financial services and royalties. A service can be exported without anything crossing a border: a Bengaluru team writing code for a US bank, or a global capability centre billing its parent abroad, both count. India is one of the world's largest services exporters, led by computer services, and its services surplus offsets a large part of its deficit in goods trade, keeping the current account deficit modest. For markets, strong services exports support the rupee and listed IT and business-services firms. Confusion to avoid: money sent home by Indians working abroad is not a services export; it is recorded separately as transfers in the current account.
example: Say in a year a country exports $400 billion of goods and imports $650 billion, a goods deficit of $250 billion, while it exports $380 billion of services and imports $200 billion. Its $180 billion services surplus covers 72% of the goods deficit.
formula: Net services = Services exports - Services imports

short: A broad trade agreement that goes beyond cutting tariffs to cover services, investment, standards and other economic cooperation between partner countries.
kid: Two friends agree not just to swap snacks freely, but also to share games, help each other with chores and follow the same playground rules.
detail: A Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) is a deeper form of free trade agreement. Besides cutting tariffs on goods, it usually covers services, investment, movement of professionals, customs procedures, standards, intellectual property and dispute settlement. The label is a matter of naming rather than law: India calls its deals with South Korea, Japan and the UAE CEPAs, its 2005 Singapore deal a CECA (Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement) and its 2025 UK deal a CETA (Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement). Under WTO rules all of them are free trade agreements. The India-UAE CEPA, in force since May 2022, removed duties on most goods over a few years. For investors, a CEPA can reshape supply chains and favour sectors such as textiles, gems and jewellery, and engineering goods. Confusion to avoid: a comprehensive deal can still exclude sensitive sectors, such as dairy for India.
example: Say a jewellery exporter sends $2 million of gold jewellery to a partner country that charged a 5% duty. Under a CEPA that removes the duty, the buyer saves $100,000 on the shipment, which lets the exporter compete more strongly on price.

short: US tariffs imposed by the President under a 1977 emergency-powers law, used in 2025 for 'reciprocal' and country-specific tariffs without a vote in Congress.
kid: The leader of a big country used a special emergency rule to put extra charges on toys coming from other countries, without waiting for everyone else to vote.
detail: The International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), passed in 1977, lets the US President regulate economic transactions after declaring a national emergency over an unusual and extraordinary foreign threat. Long used for sanctions, it was first used for tariffs by President Trump in 2025: on Canada, Mexico and China in February, citing fentanyl and migration; the across-the-board 'reciprocal' tariffs announced on 2 April 2025; and, in August 2025, an extra 25% on many Indian goods over purchases of Russian oil, taking the total to 50%. Needing no investigation or vote in Congress, these tariffs could be raised, paused or changed within days, which fed market volatility. Importers and several states challenged them; by late 2025 lower courts had ruled against the tariffs and the case was before the US Supreme Court, so check the latest status. Confusion to avoid: Section 232 and Section 301 tariffs rest on other laws.
example: Say a US importer brings in $1 million of goods that face a 2.5% normal duty plus a 25% IEEPA tariff stacked on top. The duty bill rises from $25,000 to $275,000, a cost it must absorb, pass on to customers or avoid by switching suppliers.

short: US tariffs imposed after a Commerce Department finding that imports of a product threaten national security, under Section 232 of a 1962 trade law.
kid: A country decides some things, like the metal used for building, are so important that it must make them itself. So it puts a big extra charge on that metal coming from other places.
detail: Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 lets the US President adjust imports, usually through tariffs or quotas, if a Commerce Department investigation finds they threaten to impair national security. Security is read broadly: investigations have covered steel, aluminium, cars and parts, copper, timber, semiconductors and pharmaceuticals. In 2018 the first Trump administration imposed 25% tariffs on steel and 10% on aluminium from most countries, India included, prompting retaliation. In 2025 exemptions were scrapped, aluminium rose to 25% and both metals were then raised to 50%, a 25% tariff was placed on cars and many parts, and copper products followed. Because they rest on a specific law and a formal investigation, Section 232 tariffs stand on firmer legal ground than IEEPA tariffs, and they target products rather than countries. Confusion to avoid: Section 301 is a different law, aimed at unfair trade practices.
example: Say a US firm imports steel worth $2 million. At a 25% Section 232 tariff it pays $500,000 in duty; when the rate rises to 50%, the duty doubles to $1 million, so a domestic mill charging $2.6 million, 30% above the import price, becomes cheaper than the $3 million imported cost.

short: Tariffs a country imposes on a third country's goods to punish it for trading with a sanctioned target, such as buying that target's oil.
kid: If one child is in time-out, a bigger child says anyone who keeps swapping sweets with them will have to pay extra to play with him. Many children stop swapping to avoid that.
detail: Secondary tariffs extend the logic of secondary sanctions. Primary sanctions stop a country's own firms from dealing with a target; secondary measures pressure third countries and companies to stop dealing with that target too, by threatening their access to the sanctioning country's market or financial system. Secondary sanctions usually cut a firm or bank off from dollars and US partners; secondary tariffs instead raise duties on all goods from a country that keeps trading with the target. The US introduced the tool in 2025: a March executive order allowed a 25% tariff on countries importing Venezuelan oil, and in August an extra 25% was imposed on many Indian goods over purchases of Russian oil, doubling the tariff to 50%. Such measures hit exporters with no link to the targeted trade. Confusion to avoid: a secondary tariff does not hit the targeted country directly; it hits that country's customers.
example: Say a country's exporters ship $80 billion of goods a year to a large market that already charges a 25% tariff. A 25% secondary tariff for buying a sanctioned country's oil lifts the total to 50%, and the extra duty, $20 billion a year at unchanged volumes, may far exceed the discount earned on the oil.

short: Government rules that restrict or require licences for selling certain goods, technology or software abroad, usually for national security or foreign policy reasons.
kid: Some special toys are not allowed to leave your house unless a grown-up says yes, because they could be used to hurt someone.
detail: Export controls limit what can be shipped, transferred or shared with foreign buyers, especially military and dual-use items such as advanced chips, chipmaking tools, encryption and aerospace parts. In the US, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security runs them, and its Entity List names foreign firms that need a licence, usually denied, before receiving controlled items. Since October 2022 the US has steadily tightened rules on advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment sold to China. China has replied with controls on gallium, germanium, graphite and rare earths. India runs its own regime through the SCOMET list of sensitive goods and technologies, and has also curbed some farm exports to protect domestic supply. For investors, controls can shrink a chip firm's market overnight and push supply chains to relocate. Confusion to avoid: export controls restrict who may buy, not the price, so they are not tariffs.
example: Say a chip designer earns $10 billion a year, with 15% of sales going to customers that a new rule places on a restricted list. If no licences are granted, $1.5 billion of annual revenue is at risk unless it finds other buyers.

short: Penalties such as trade bans, asset freezes and finance restrictions that governments impose on countries, firms or people to change their behaviour.
kid: If a child keeps breaking the rules, the other children stop playing and sharing toys with them until they behave better.
detail: Economic sanctions are penalties imposed for foreign policy or security goals, short of military force. They include trade embargoes, bans on specific goods, asset freezes, exclusion from financial systems and payment networks such as SWIFT, and limits on investment or technology. Sanctions may cover a whole country or target named people, firms and ships. In the US, the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) keeps the Specially Designated Nationals list; the UN, EU and UK run their own regimes. After Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Western countries froze roughly half of Russia's central bank reserves and later capped the price of Russian oil, which reshaped oil trade and made India a major buyer of discounted Russian crude. For companies and banks, sanctions mean compliance screening and the risk of heavy fines. Confusion to avoid: India formally enforces only UN sanctions, but its banks often heed US ones.
example: Say a refiner buys 1 million barrels of crude at a $10 discount to an assumed market price of $75, paying $65 a barrel. It saves $10 million, but if a sanctions breach brings a $50 million fine, the penalty wipes out the saving five times over.

short: Moving supply chains and production to politically friendly countries to reduce dependence on rivals, even if costs are somewhat higher.
kid: Instead of getting your crayons from a child who sometimes refuses to share, you get them from your good friends, even if it means giving a little more in return.
detail: Friend-shoring means moving sourcing and manufacturing to allied or trusted countries, so that geopolitical shocks, sanctions or export bans by rivals cannot easily cut off supplies. The term spread in 2022, after pandemic disruptions and Russia's invasion of Ukraine exposed concentrated supply chains. Related ideas differ: reshoring or onshoring brings production back home, nearshoring moves it to nearby countries such as Mexico for the US, and China plus one adds a second source outside China rather than leaving it entirely. India pitches itself as a friend-shoring destination, backed by Production Linked Incentive schemes, and electronics is a visible case, with global smartphone brands expanding assembly in India for export. The cost is efficiency: duplicating supply chains raises prices and may add to inflation over time. Confusion to avoid: friend-shoring is not the same as deglobalisation, because trade often keeps growing, just along different routes.
example: Say a firm buys a component for $10 from a rival country or $11.50 from a friendly one. Switching 1 million units a year raises costs by $1.5 million, a 15% premium it pays as insurance against supply being cut off.

short: A slowdown or reversal in global integration, as trade, investment and supply chains grow more slowly than the world economy or retreat behind borders.
kid: Children in different houses used to share toys every day. Now each house keeps more toys at home and shares less with the others.
detail: Deglobalisation describes countries becoming less economically connected: trade grows more slowly than world output, cross-border investment falls and supply chains shorten or regionalise. After rising fast from the 1990s to 2008, world trade as a share of GDP has broadly plateaued, a pattern dubbed slowbalisation. The IMF uses geoeconomic fragmentation for the policy-driven version, where trade splits into blocs because of tariffs, sanctions, export controls and industrial subsidies, and has estimated that severe fragmentation could cost several percent of global output. Drivers include US-China rivalry, the pandemic, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the US tariffs of 2025. For India, fragmentation is both a risk, as higher barriers hurt a trade-reliant services exporter, and an opportunity, as firms diversify away from China. Confusion to avoid: trade can still hit records in dollar terms while the world deglobalises relative to output.
example: Say world exports plus imports grow from $60 trillion to $62 trillion while world GDP grows from $100 trillion to $106 trillion. Trade rises in dollars, but trade openness falls from 60% to about 58.5%, a sign of slowbalisation.

short: A rupee account an Indian bank keeps for a foreign bank, letting traders settle cross-border trade in rupees rather than dollars.
kid: Two friends from different towns keep a jar of your town's coins at your house. When they swap toys, they just move coins in that jar instead of using a third kind of money.
detail: Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVAs) are the core of an RBI framework, introduced in July 2022, for invoicing, paying and settling exports and imports in rupees. An authorised Indian bank opens a rupee account for a correspondent bank of the partner country. Indian importers pay rupees into it and Indian exporters are paid out of it, so trade can be settled without converting through dollars. Surplus balances can be invested in Indian government securities. The aims are to cut conversion costs and currency risk, widen use of the rupee and keep trade going with partners short of dollars or under sanctions; banks from Russia, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, the UAE and many other countries have opened SRVAs. Use has been modest, because partners with trade surpluses against India pile up rupees they cannot easily spend. Confusion to avoid: vostro means 'your account with us'; nostro means 'our account with you'.
example: Say an Indian importer owes a Sri Lankan supplier ₹50 lakh. It pays its Indian bank, which credits the Sri Lankan bank's SRVA, and no dollars are involved; if each currency conversion would have cost 0.5%, skipping two saves about ₹50,000.

short: A group of major emerging economies, originally Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, that coordinates on trade, finance and global governance.
kid: It is a club of big friends from different parts of the world who meet to help each other and to get more say in the playground's rules.
detail: BRICS began as BRIC, a 2001 label coined by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill for large, fast-growing emerging markets. Brazil, Russia, India and China held their first leaders' summit in 2009, South Africa joined in 2010, and the group expanded in 2024 with Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE, followed by Indonesia in 2025, while Saudi Arabia has been invited. It created the New Development Bank, based in Shanghai, and a Contingent Reserve Arrangement for emergency liquidity. Members discuss settling trade in local currencies and linking payment systems, but there is no BRICS currency and no agreed plan for one, and India has said de-dollarisation is not its policy. The expanded group covers a large share of world population and output but is politically diverse, with rivals such as India and China inside it. Confusion to avoid: BRICS is not a free trade area; members charge each other normal tariffs.
example: Say two BRICS members trade $10 billion a year and settle 20% of it in their own currencies instead of dollars. That moves $2 billion out of dollar settlement and saves on conversion costs, but the other $8 billion still runs through dollars.

short: Foreign direct investment coming into a country minus money foreign investors take back out and minus direct investment the country's own firms make abroad.
kid: New friends bring toys to share in your playroom, some friends take their toys back home, and you also take some toys to their houses. What stays in your playroom at the end is what counts.
detail: Gross FDI inflows measure new long-term investment by foreigners, such as building factories or buying 10% or more of a company. Net FDI subtracts repatriation and disinvestment, when foreign owners sell stakes or take capital home, and, in balance of payments data, outward FDI by domestic firms investing abroad. The RBI reports gross inflows, net inward FDI and net FDI after outward investment. The gap matters because a strong gross number can hide a fall in capital that actually stays. In 2024-25, India's gross FDI inflows stayed high, but net FDI fell close to zero as private equity funds and multinationals sold stakes, often through IPOs and block deals, and Indian firms invested more abroad. Exits are not all bad: they show investors can realise gains, which can attract new money. Confusion to avoid: profits sent home as dividends are counted in the current account, not as FDI outflows.
example: Say gross FDI inflows are $80 billion, repatriation and disinvestment are $50 billion and outward FDI by domestic firms is $29 billion. Net inward FDI is $30 billion, but net FDI is only $1 billion, so very little of the gross inflow adds to the country's capital account.
formula: Net FDI = Gross FDI inflows - Repatriation and disinvestment - Outward FDI by residents

short: A large, rapid outflow of money from a country as investors and residents lose confidence in its economy, currency or politics.
kid: When people hear a storm is coming to their town, they quickly carry their piggy banks to a safer town. If too many do it at once, the town has very little left.
detail: Capital flight is a sudden, large movement of money out of a country by foreign investors and often by residents, driven by fear of devaluation, default, high inflation, confiscation, capital controls or political turmoil. It shows up as falling reserves, a sliding currency, rising bond yields and sometimes deposit withdrawals. A sudden stop, a term popularised by Guillermo Calvo, is the related case where foreign inflows financing a current account deficit dry up, forcing a sharp cut in spending and imports. Examples include Mexico in 1994, East Asia in 1997-98 and Russia in 2014 and 2022. India's 1991 crisis involved a drying up of external credit and withdrawals of deposits by non-resident Indians. Governments respond with rate hikes, reserve sales, IMF support or capital controls, and fear of controls can trigger more flight. Confusion to avoid: routine portfolio outflows are not capital flight; flight implies panic and lost confidence.
example: Say a country holds $60 billion of reserves and investors pull out $4 billion a month. After six months reserves are down to $36 billion, a 40% drop, which is why central banks often raise rates sharply or seek IMF help well before reserves run out.
